expected_evidence: Geochemical assays (Ir, Pt, Os, other platinum-group elements) from Younger Dryas boundary (YDB) sediment layers across multiple European sites showing background-level (non-anomalous) concentrations
Independent replication attempts (or failures to replicate) of the original iridium-anomaly claims, published as peer-reviewed critiques
Lake/peat sediment or ice-core proxy records spanning ~10,900 cal BC without a corresponding iridium/platinum spike
Absence of confirmed hypervelocity-impact indicators (shocked quartz, high-temperature melt spherules, nanodiamonds) in independently re-analyzed YDB samples
Astronomical/geophysical surveys failing to identify a corresponding impact crater or airburst structure of appropriate age in or near Europe
Statistical/methodological critique literature (e.g., contamination, misidentification of magnetic/carbon spherules, analytical artifacts) explaining the original anomaly reports
Meta-analyses or consensus statements from the geoscience community treating the impact hypothesis as unsupported
response.rationale: This hypothesis concerns a refutation event dated to the Younger Dryas onset. The relevant evidence classes are geological (sediment/ice-core geochemistry, spherule/nanodiamond analyses) and astronomical (crater/airburst search, bolide modeling), both of which have comparatively high detectability for this period (0.65 and 0.7 respectively in the table), since modern high-precision mass spectrometry and dating techniques can resolve trace-element anomalies (or their absence) in well-preserved sediment cores tens of thousands of years old. Material archaeological evidence (0.35) and genetic evidence (0.3) are secondary and less diagnostic for a refutation of a specific geochemical anomaly claim. Because the underlying scientific debate (Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis) is a documented, recent (post-2007) controversy with an extensive published literature of both original claims and rebuttals, the refutation itself is highly detectable as a matter of historical/scientific record — this is not a case where a low detectability score should be invoked to explain silence. I weight the adjustment toward the geological/astronomical channels (primary evidentiary basis for confirming or refuting an iridium anomaly) while discounting slightly for the weaker material/genetic/textual channels, yielding an overall adjustment around 0.6. Note: my characterization of the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis debate and its critique literature draws on model-prior (unverified, recalled-from-training) knowledge rather than the evidence text provided, and should be treated accordingly.
